title: What are Hadith and Sunnah?
summary: The second source of Islamic guidance alongside the Quran: what hadith and Sunnah are, and how scholars judge their reliability.

body.text: The previous lesson covered the Quran, God's revealed word. Muslims rely on a second source alongside it: the Sunnah, the example of Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) — what he said, did, and approved of. A hadith is a single reported record of that example: a specific saying or action, passed down with a chain of narrators back to the Prophet. Together, the Quran and the Sunnah make up the two sources Muslims turn to for how to pray, worship, and live.
Why a second source is needed

The Quran tells Muslims to pray, but doesn't spell out the exact movements and words — that level of detail comes from the Sunnah, from watching how the Prophet himself prayed and taught his companions to pray. This pattern repeats across worship and daily life: the Quran gives the command and the principle, and the Sunnah shows the lived example of how to carry it out.

body.arabic: لَقَدْ كَانَ لَكُمْ فِي رَسُولِ اللَّهِ أُسْوَةٌ حَسَنَةٌ
body.translation: Indeed in the Messenger of Allah you have a good example to follow.

body.text: How hadith are checked for reliability

Not every reported saying is treated as equally certain. Early scholars built a careful discipline around examining each hadith's chain of narrators — who reported it, from whom, and whether each link was known to be trustworthy and accurate — and grading the result. "Sahih" (authentic) and "hasan" (good) are the two grades solid enough to build guidance on; "da'if" (weak) hadith are treated with caution or set aside. Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim are the two most rigorously verified collections, widely considered the most reliable after the Quran itself.

body.question: Do I need to memorise hadith collections to be a good Muslim?
body.answer: No. Scholars spend lifetimes on this so ordinary Muslims don't have to verify every chain of narration themselves. It's enough to know the basic idea — that authenticity is checked — and to lean on trustworthy teachers and collections rather than sourcing hadith from unverified social media posts.

body.question: What if a hadith seems to contradict the Quran?
body.answer: The Quran always takes precedence, and a hadith judged as weak or contradicting a clear Quranic principle is set aside. In practice this is rare in the well-established, authenticated collections — genuine tensions are usually a matter of a hadith's specific context or a weaker grading, which is exactly the kind of question worth asking a knowledgeable teacher.

body.question: The Wudu and Salah steps you've been learning in this app come from the Sunnah as much as the Quran. Does knowing there's a documented, checked chain behind them change how you think about following them?
